intro: A horn player takes the floor in the enormous central dance of Mahler’s Fifth. Country Ländler and Viennese waltz trip over one another, then stop for a horn call that seems to come from far outside the ballroom.

sections.label: A · Horn call and country dance
sections.mNote: The tune is tossed between solo horn, woodwinds and violins

sections.label: B · A violin waltz in B♭
sections.mNote: A gentler melody above plucked strings

sections.label: A′ · The opening call interrupts
sections.mNote: The call returns, followed by racing string entries

sections.label: C · The horn sings at length
sections.mNote: Long horn phrases lead into quiet plucked-string exchanges

sections.label: Dev · Brass figures and running strings
sections.mNote: The dance tunes crowd together before the opening returns

sections.label: A″ · The D-major dance returns
sections.mNote: Old tunes meet new string runs and wind replies

sections.label: C′ · The horn solo returns
sections.mNote: The obbligato horn takes up its long phrase again

sections.label: Coda · Running strings and final horn calls
sections.mNote: Dotted calls and running scales drive to two short chords

cues.title: A horn takes the floor
cues.text: Three notes from the horns set the dance going. Mahler gives one player a separate corno obbligato part: a soloist inside the orchestra. Marked Kräftig, nicht zu schnell — vigorous, not too fast — in three-four and D major, the opening tosses its tune between the solo horn, the woodwinds and the first violins.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 118: Kräftig, nicht zu schnell; D major, 3/4; a separate staff for Corno obligato in F beside the four horns, whose first bars rise in three-note gestures. Bettie Jo Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide has a playful tune delicately tossed between a solo French horn, the woodwinds and the first violins: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A man in the full light of day
cues.text: Natalie Bauer-Lechner reports Mahler’s idea for the scherzo: “a human being in the full light of day, in the prime of his life”. After the funeral march and the storm, the Fifth turns to the open air.
cues.evidence: The Aspen Music Festival programme note gives Bauer-Lechner’s report of Mahler’s idea for the character of the scherzo: https://www.aspenmusicfestival.com/program_notes/view/mahler-symphony-no.-5-in-c-sharp-minor . Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide quotes Mahler to Bauer-Lechner on 25 July 1901 about the same movement (“a human being in the full light of day”): https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/

cues.title: Violins with a lilt
cues.text: The first violins start a softer waltz in B♭ major. Much of the accompaniment is plucked, leaving the tune room for its little hesitations: Mahler’s footnote asks for the eighth note in the motive to be played always a little fleetingly, a little carelessly. The marking is Etwas ruhiger — a little calmer.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 128, rehearsal 6: Etwas ruhiger; two flats; first violins carry the tune over pizzicato violas and basses; footnote “In diesem Motiv ist das Achtel stets etwas flüchtig-nachlässig auszuführen”. Basinger: the first trio is a clear waltz, a relaxed passage with a temporary relaxation of tempo: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The call cuts in
cues.text: The opening horn call interrupts the waltz at fff. Soon the strings chase one another through a fugato, each entry diving in while the earlier line is still running, and Mahler writes wild! over the entries.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 132, rehearsal 8: horn call fff, then the running figure entering in violins, violas, cellos and basses, with wild! over successive entries. Basinger: the scherzo leads to a brief yet brisk fugue that ushers in the second trio: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Themes side by side
cues.text: Recovering from surgery in March 1901, Mahler tells Natalie Bauer-Lechner of his dream of themes that “develop freely, side by side, each with its own impetus and purpose”.
cues.evidence: The Aspen Music Festival programme note reports the conversations with Natalie Bauer-Lechner in March 1901 and quotes the remark: https://www.aspenmusicfestival.com/program_notes/view/mahler-symphony-no.-5-in-c-sharp-minor

cues.title: A horn beyond the ballroom
cues.text: The solo horn sings a slow, spacious song, marked Tempo (poco sostenuto). Its phrases linger — lang, verklingend, dying away — and stop short on fermatas while English horn, bass clarinet, bassoons and low strings answer.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), pp. 136–137: four horns with bells in the air (Schalltrichter in die Höhe), the obbligato horn with rit. and molto portamento, then Tempo (poco sostenuto) with lang and verklingend in the horn part and answering English horn, bass clarinet, bassoons, violas, cellos and basses. Basinger: the second trio’s rocking theme, most prominently in an unaccompanied horn solo: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bach on the shelves
cues.text: Mahler subscribes to the collected edition of Bach’s works. In the Fifth, tunes begin to run alongside one another with a new persistence: the scherzo’s strings can keep their own dance going underneath the horn’s.
cues.evidence: Mahler Foundation, Symphony No. 5 introduction, on the Bach edition and the growing role of counterpoint in the scherzo and finale. https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-introduction/

cues.title: The dance is plucked
cues.text: At rehearsal 11, Molto moderato, solo violins, cellos and basses pluck fragments of the dance. Without the bows sustaining them, the phrases seem to tiptoe from note to note. A tune that filled the orchestra now fits into the gaps between a few players.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 137, rehearsal 11: Molto moderato, violins, cellos and basses marked Solo pizz. Basinger: Mahler explores the second trio’s theme through variation and fragmentation: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Snippets for chamber groups
cues.text: The second trio’s music is broken into pieces for small groups. Oboe, bassoons, trumpet and tuba each take a quiet turn, marked p espress., over sustained strings and a timpani roll, and the themes pass from group to group.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 140: oboe, bassoons, trumpet and tuba each marked p espress., long string notes and a timpani roll beneath. Basinger: Mahler sets the rocking theme against itself and amid materials from the first trio: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Fifty years too early
cues.text: Rehearsing in Cologne in October 1904, Mahler writes to Alma that conductors for the next fifty years “will all take it too fast and make nonsense of it”. He wishes he could give the symphony “its first performance fifty years after my death”.
cues.evidence: Peoria Symphony Orchestra’s programme essay quotes Mahler’s letter to Alma written during the rehearsals for the première: https://peoriasymphony.org/digging-deeper-into-mahlers-fifth/ . The Mahler Foundation’s concert record for Cologne, 18 October 1904: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/locations/germany/cologne/1904-concert-cologne-18-10-1904/

cues.title: The tune darkens
cues.text: The solo horn announces a new section. The scherzo tune comes back in a minor key, four flats, growing quicker, louder and more thickly scored, its shape taking on the contours of the first trio’s waltz.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), pp. 140–145: four flats, the obbligato horn entering f at the end of p. 140, the crescendo to p. 145. Basinger: the solo horn announces the new section; the scherzo melody in a minor key, gradually faster, loud and thicker, takes on the contours of the first trio’s waltz: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The brass cast the daydream aside
cues.text: Mahler marks the page Nicht schleppen — don’t drag. Bassoons, trombones, tuba and basses repeat a short running figure, trumpets cut across it, woodwinds trill and the glockenspiel rings above.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 145: Nicht schleppen; four flats; the running figure in bassoons, contrabassoon, trombones, tuba and basses, trumpets repeating a short figure, trills in flutes, oboes and clarinets, glockenspiel ff.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: D major, crowded again
cues.text: A halt, then rehearsal 17: the four flats give way to D major and the opening horn call returns, marked poco rit. a tempo I. The scherzo starts over, its tunes crowded together again.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 148, rehearsal 17: change of key signature from four flats to two sharps, poco rit. a tempo I., horn call in the four horns and the obbligato horn. Basinger: after the sudden halt the composer starts to recapitulate the scherzo’s material as at the movement’s outset: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The horn keeps trying
cues.text: The obbligato horn sings its long phrase again, but the pace keeps changing around it: Langsam, a tempo (schnell), rit., a tempo. Over the horn’s line Mahler writes nicht zurückhalten! — don’t hold back — while the strings tremble beneath.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 170: obbligato horn with nicht riten and nicht zurückhalten!, Langsam, a tempo (schnell), rit., a tempo; strings trem. Basinger: the coda brings back the rocking theme in another lengthy horn solo, after which a sudden increase in tempo hastens the scherzo to its end: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One last turn
cues.text: At rehearsal 32 winds, brass and violins call fff in dotted rhythms over running scales in violas, cellos and basses. The score drives to the end Sehr drängend bis zum Schluss — very pressing to the close — and the dance stops on two short fff chords.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), pp. 176–177: rehearsal 32, dotted figures in woodwinds, horns, trumpets and violins, running scales in violas, cellos and basses; p. 177 Sehr drängend bis zum Schluss, last two bars two short fff chords. Basinger: a sudden increase in tempo hastens the scherzo to its end: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: B♭ major, with plucked strings
transitions.from: A · Horn call and country dance
transitions.to: B · A violin waltz in B♭
transitions.how: The busy dance breaks off in horn and trumpet calls fading to pp. At Etwas ruhiger the key signature turns to two flats, and the first violins begin the waltz above plucked violas and basses, with half the cellos bowing a separate line.
transitions.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 128, rehearsal 6: calls in horns and trumpets ff to pp, Etwas ruhiger, two flats, pizzicato violas and basses, cellos die Hälfte arco.

transitions.title: The trumpet interrupts the waltz
transitions.from: B · A violin waltz in B♭
transitions.how: The opening horn call breaks in at fff and the dance returns in D major. The running string figure then enters in one part after another, each marked wild!, turning the accompaniment into a fugato.
transitions.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 132, rehearsal 8: horn call fff, running figure in successive string entries marked wild!. Basinger: a brief yet brisk fugue.

transitions.title: Repeated horn notes become a song
transitions.to: C · The horn sings at length
transitions.how: The four horns enter one after another on the same held note, bells raised, over fff string chords. The solo horn takes the line with a rit. and molto portamento, and the music slows into Tempo (poco sostenuto).
transitions.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), pp. 136–137: Schalltrichter in die Höhe in the four horns, fff string chords, obbligato horn rit. and molto portamento, Tempo (poco sostenuto).

transitions.title: The first call restores D major
transitions.from: Dev · Brass figures and running strings
transitions.how: The music halts on a breath mark. At rehearsal 17 the four flats become D major, and the opening horn call cuts back in, marked poco rit. a tempo I.
transitions.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), pp. 145–148: Nicht schleppen (p. 145), breath marks and the change of key signature at rehearsal 17 (p. 148). Basinger: a sudden halt, then the scherzo is recapitulated as at the outset.

transitions.title: The bass drum starts the dance
transitions.to: Coda · Running strings and final horn calls
transitions.how: The pace quickens at a tempo (schnell) over a bass-drum roll and string tremolos. At rehearsal 32 the woodwinds, brass and violins call in dotted rhythms over running scales in the lower strings, and the music drives to the end.
transitions.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), pp. 170–177: a tempo (schnell), bass-drum roll, string tremolos (p. 170); rehearsal 32 (p. 176); Sehr drängend bis zum Schluss (p. 177).

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 5, III, Peters study score, plate 9015
source.locator: Printed pp. 118–177. The separate obbligato horn leads the opening; p. 128 introduces the gentler waltz; pp. 136–142 give the horn and pizzicato episodes; pp. 172–177 bring back the dance figures.

timeline.note: The horn call opens into the obbligato horn’s dance, with answers across the orchestra.
Violins lead the gentler waltz above bassoon and plucked strings.
The obbligato horn stretches its phrase as the accompaniment falls away.
Plucked strings exchange little pieces of the dance.
Woodwind melodies pass above changing groups of brass and strings.
Strings keep their separate dancing lines beneath wind and brass calls.
Clarinets and horns exchange phrases as the strings begin moving again.
Horn calls and running strings gather the orchestra for the close.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
